title: Nuclides, isotopes and atomic mass
prior_knowledge_summary: The nucleus is very small, positively charged and contains nearly all atomic mass.
Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus, while electrons orbit outside it.
new_learning: Distinguish proton number Z from nucleon number A and calculate neutron number A - Z.
Read and write nuclide notation and identify isotopes.
Use the unified atomic mass unit u as a unit of nuclear and atomic mass.

learning_outcomes.text: Distinguish between nucleon number and proton number.
Understand that isotopes are forms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons in their nuclei.
Use the unified atomic mass unit (u) as a unit of mass.

blocks.heading: How can two atoms be the same element but have different masses?
content: Imagine two neutral atoms that behave as the same element. Each has 17 protons, yet one nucleus contains 18 neutrons and the other contains 20. Their chemical identity agrees, but their masses do not.
We need a label that keeps two counts separate: the count that fixes the element and the count that describes the whole nucleus.

figure.purpose: Create the isotope puzzle by comparing equal proton counts with unequal neutron counts.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch of two enlarged nuclei. Each has 17 red proton dots; one has 18 grey neutron dots and the other 20. Show identical simple electron shells but do not name isotopes or display nuclide notation.
figure.alt_text: Two atoms have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

blocks.heading: Two numbers describe one nucleus
content: The proton number Z is the number of protons in the nucleus. Because the number of protons fixes the element, changing Z means changing the element.
The nucleon number A is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. Protons and neutrons are both nucleons. Therefore neutron number = A - Z.
For a nucleus with A = 31 and Z = 15, the proton count is 15 and the neutron count is 31 - 15 = 16. Check: 15 + 16 = 31 nucleons.

figure.purpose: Separate the meanings of A and Z and show neutron subtraction.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper annotated nucleus with braces: Z points only to red proton dots, A encloses all proton and neutron dots, and a short side calculation shows neutrons = A - Z. Use A = 31 and Z = 15.
figure.alt_text: A nucleus diagram distinguishes proton number Z from total nucleon number A.

blocks.heading: Read nuclide notation like a compact address
content: A nuclide is represented as ^A_Z X. The element symbol X identifies the element, A at the upper left is the nucleon number, and Z at the lower left is the proton number.
For ^{27}_{13}Al, X is Al, A = 27 and Z = 13. Its nucleus has 13 protons and 27 - 13 = 14 neutrons.
The positions are not interchangeable. Since A counts protons plus neutrons, A cannot be smaller than Z. That is a quick reasonableness check.

figure.purpose: Teach the spatial reading of nuclide notation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper notation map centred on 27 over 13 beside Al. Use arrows to label upper-left A as nucleon number, lower-left Z as proton number and Al as element symbol. Add a small 13 p plus 14 n check below.
figure.alt_text: Nuclide notation for aluminium-27 labels nucleon number, proton number and element symbol.

blocks.heading: Build a nuclide label from particle counts
content: A nucleus contains 26 protons and 30 neutrons. First use the proton count to identify the element: Z = 26 corresponds to Fe. Next count every nucleon: A = 26 + 30 = 56. The notation is ^{56}_{26}Fe.
Read the label backward as an independent check. It gives 26 protons and 56 - 26 = 30 neutrons, matching the starting nucleus.
Notice the order of thought: proton count chooses X and Z; total nuclear particle count chooses A.

figure.purpose: Model the complete route from particle counts to nuclide notation and back-check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked flow with four boxes: 26 protons gives Z = 26, periodic-table tile gives Fe, 26 + 30 gives A = 56, final nuclide notation. Add reverse check 56 - 26 = 30.
figure.alt_text: A worked flow converts 26 protons and 30 neutrons into iron-56 nuclide notation.

blocks.heading: Isotopes keep Z but change A
content: Isotopes are forms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons in their nuclei. The same element means the same proton number Z. Different neutron counts make the nucleon numbers A different.
For example, ^{20}_{10}Ne and ^{22}_{10}Ne are isotopes. Both have 10 protons, so both are neon. Their neutron counts are 10 and 12, so their nucleon numbers differ.
A useful test is: compare Z first. If Z differs, the pair cannot be isotopes of the same element. If Z matches, compare A or neutron number.

figure.purpose: Make isotope classification a visible compare-Z-then-A procedure.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison table for neon-20 and neon-22 with rows for Z, A, protons and neutrons. Highlight equal Z in one colour and unequal neutron count in another.
figure.alt_text: A table shows that neon-20 and neon-22 have equal proton numbers but different neutron numbers.

blocks.heading: Heavier does not mean a different element
content: It can feel natural to name an atom by its total number of nuclear particles. That would make a heavier nucleus seem like a new element. The idea fails because element identity follows proton number, not nucleon number.

Adding a neutron changes A and usually changes the mass, but it leaves Z unchanged. The atom is then a different isotope of the same element. Adding a proton would change Z and therefore change the element.

figure.purpose: Repair confusion between changing neutron count and changing element identity.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper fork diagram from one nucleus. Branch one adds a grey neutron and is labelled same element, different isotope. Branch two adds a red proton and is labelled different element. Do not introduce decay arrows.
figure.alt_text: Adding a neutron keeps the element the same, while adding a proton changes the element.

blocks.heading: Use u when nuclear masses are tiny
content: The unified atomic mass unit, symbol u, is a convenient unit for atomic and nuclear masses. Use the stated conversion 1 u = 1.66 × 10^-27 kg when moving between u and kilograms.
A nucleus of mass 6.64 × 10^-26 kg has mass (6.64 × 10^-26) / (1.66 × 10^-27) = 40.0 u. Check the powers: 10^-26 divided by 10^-27 contributes a factor of 10, and 6.64 / 1.66 = 4, giving 40.

The complete bookkeeping route is now short: read Z for protons and element identity, read A for total nucleons, calculate neutrons using A - Z, and compare equal Z with different A to identify isotopes. Keep radiation and decay rules for the next module.

figure.purpose: Combine notation, isotope comparison and mass-unit conversion into one boundary-safe summary.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper summary board with three zones: annotated nuclide notation, equal-Z isotope test, and a kg divided by 1.66 × 10^-27 conversion arrow to u. Keep radiation and decay absent.
figure.alt_text: A summary links nuclide notation, isotope identification and conversion of a tiny mass into unified atomic mass units.

evidence_basis.p1_status: deferred by canonical lesson specification; no lesson assignment invented

misconceptions_addressed: A different nucleon number always means a different element.
The upper and lower numbers in nuclide notation can be exchanged.
next_lesson_can_assume: Z is proton number and fixes element identity.
A is the total number of protons and neutrons.
Isotopes have the same Z but different neutron numbers.
Nuclide notation and u can be read and used.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Nuclear decay equations or conservation rules.
